At the height of Trump's trade war with China, tariffs were being imposed almost weekly, and companies like Logitech promptly raised the prices of products sold in the United States significantly.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. Yet so far, no company has been seen passing refunds on to consumers, and class-action lawsuits have been filed demanding the situation be rectified...

Trump tariff saga

Trump made a big deal last year about the U.S. trade deficit with China, apparently fantasising that slapping heavy tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the United States.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The U.S. lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, and cheap labour needed to support large-scale consumer electronics production for major brands.

Trump has consistently claimed that China paid the tariffs, but the reality is that U.S. brands absorbed the costs themselves when importing Chinese-made finished goods, then passed them on to consumers through price hikes. Tariff rates at the peak of the saga soared as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example — the company raised prices on roughly half its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and ordered that amounts already paid by U.S. businesses be refunded. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, yet the affected companies have still not announced any plans to refund customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking refunds for consumers who paid inflated prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's view

The principle here is beyond dispute: companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to customers, and are now getting the money back from the government. Morally speaking, they ought to return this money to the consumers who bought their products during this period.

In practical terms, however, this would be extremely difficult. Logitech would need to identify every single transaction made through its vast third-party retail network, record what consumers actually paid, and calculate how much of that was attributable to tariffs.

Even if the lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a rather interesting precedent — though it must be noted that in class-action suits, the biggest beneficiaries are usually the lawyers, while ordinary consumers typically end up with only a negligible share.
